claim: Aedes aegypti is the principal mosquito vector for many arboviruses including yellow fever, chikungunya, dengue, and Zika.
source: Aedes aegypti is the principal mosquito vector of several arboviruses, including yellow fever, chikungunya, dengue, and Zika (Scott and Takken, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scott and Takken, 2012

claim: Aedes aegypti places roughly half of the world's population at risk of acquiring vector-borne diseases.
source: This mosquito alone places roughly half of the world's population at risk of acquiring vector-borne diseases while causing an estimated 390 million dengue infections annually (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013

claim: Aedes aegypti causes an estimated 390 million dengue infections annually.
source: This mosquito alone places roughly half of the world's population at risk of acquiring vector-borne diseases while causing an estimated 390 million dengue infections annually (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013

claim: Traditional mosquito control strategies have significantly reduced mosquito-borne disease burdens.
source: Traditional mosquito control strategies, including long-lasting insecticide-treated bed nets (LLINs), chemical insecticides, and environmental management (Schreck, 1991), have significantly reduced mosquito-borne disease burdens
evidence: Supported by citation to Schreck, 1991

claim: Traditional mosquito control interventions are largely unsustainable due to the development of both genetic and behavioral vector resistance.
source: however these interventions are largely unsustainable due to the development of both genetic and behavioral vector resistance that decrease their efficacy (Vontas et al., 2012), high costs, and the need for repeated applications with limited spatial impact.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vontas et al., 2012

claim: Chemical interventions negatively affect non-target beneficial organisms, such as pollinators.
source: Furthermore, chemical interventions, a fundamental tool for vector control, negatively affect non-target beneficial organisms, such as pollinators.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about chemical intervention impacts

claim: Wolbachia incompatible insect technique (IIT) is currently being implemented on a small-scale in the field to control populations of Ae. aegypti.
source: Species-specific mosquito population suppression technologies, such as the Wolbachia incompatible insect technique (IIT) and the release of dominant lethal gene (RIDL), are currently being implemented on a small-scale in the field to control populations of Ae. aegypti (Harris et al., 2012; McMeniman et al., 2009; Phuc et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2012; McMeniman et al., 2009; Phuc et al., 2007

claim: Release of dominant lethal gene (RIDL) is currently being implemented on a small-scale in the field to control populations of Ae. aegypti.
source: Species-specific mosquito population suppression technologies, such as the Wolbachia incompatible insect technique (IIT) and the release of dominant lethal gene (RIDL), are currently being implemented on a small-scale in the field to control populations of Ae. aegypti (Harris et al., 2012; McMeniman et al., 2009; Phuc et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2012; McMeniman et al., 2009; Phuc et al., 2007

claim: IIT and RIDL technologies require continuous inundation, which is laborious and cost prohibitive to many areas with the largest vector-borne disease burdens.
source: While these technologies improve Ae. aegypti control capabilities, they require continuous inundation, which is laborious and cost prohibitive to many areas with the largest vector-borne disease burdens.
evidence: Statement based on inference from the nature of these technologies

claim: Certain Wolbachia strains can spread to fixation while reducing the vector's susceptibility to dengue virus.
source: In addition to IIT, Wolbachia has also been used for population replacement in various locations (Hoffmann et al., 2011; Jiggins, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2017), as certain strains can spread to fixation while reducing the vector's susceptibility to dengue virus (Walker et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2011; Jiggins, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2011

claim: The effectiveness of different Wolbachia strains varies so far as to even enhance vector competence in some contexts.
source: However, the literature suggests the effectiveness of different Wolbachia strains varies so far as to even enhance vector competence in some contexts, which may lead to a reevaluation of this technique (Amuzu et al., 2018; Dodson et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2012; King et al., 2018; Murdock et al., 2015; Zélé et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Amuzu et al., 2018; Dodson et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2012; King et al., 2018; Murdock et al., 2015; Zélé et al., 2014

claim: Homing-based gene-drive technologies can expedite the elimination and eradication of vector-borne diseases.
source: One innovative technology, first articulated by Burt (2003), utilizes homing-based gene-drive technologies to expedite the elimination and eradication of vector-borne diseases (Burt, 2014; Champer et al., 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014; Marshall and Akbari, 2017; Marshall and Akbari, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burt, 2003; Burt, 2014; Champer et al., 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014; Marshall and Akbari, 2017; Marshall and Akbari, 2016

claim: Gene drives function by exploiting the organism's innate DNA repair machinery to copy or 'home' themselves into a target genomic location prior to meiosis in the germline.
source: Conceptually, these drives function by exploiting the organism's innate DNA repair machinery to copy or 'home' themselves into a target genomic location prior to meiosis in the germline.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about gene drive mechanism

claim: Gene drives convert wild type alleles into drive alleles in heterozygotes, thereby forcing super-Mendelian inheritance of the drive into subsequent generations.
source: This process converts wild type alleles into drive alleles in heterozygotes, thereby forcing super-Mendelian inheritance of the drive into subsequent generations, irrespective of the fitness cost to the organism.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about gene drive mechanism

claim: Gene drives can spread the drive and any linked anti-pathogen 'cargo genes,' to fixation in a population in a short time frame.
source: Theoretically, this inheritance scheme can spread the drive and any linked anti-pathogen 'cargo genes,' to fixation in a population in a short time frame (Buchman et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2018), even with modest introduction frequencies (Burt, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buchman et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2018; Burt, 2003

claim: CRISPR-based homing gene drives have been developed in yeast.
source: In fact, proof-of-concept CRISPR-based homing gene drives have recently been developed in several organisms including yeast (Basgall et al., 2018; DiCarlo et al., 2015; Roggenkamp et al., 2018; Shapiro et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Basgall et al., 2018; DiCarlo et al., 2015; Roggenkamp et al., 2018; Shapiro et al., 2018

claim: CRISPR-based homing gene drives have been developed in flies.
source: flies (Champer et al., 2019; Champer et al., 2018; Champer et al., 2017; Kandul et al., 2019a; KaramiNejadRanjbar et al., 2018; Oberhofer et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Champer et al., 2019; Champer et al., 2018; Champer et al., 2017; Kandul et al., 2019a; KaramiNejadRanjbar et al., 2018; Oberhofer et al., 2018

claim: CRISPR-based homing gene drives have been developed in mice.
source: mice (Grunwald et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Grunwald et al., 2019

claim: CRISPR-based homing gene drives have been developed in Anopheles gambiae.
source: and two malaria vector species, Anopheles gambiae (Hammond et al., 2016; Hammond et al., 2017; Kyrou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2016; Hammond et al., 2017; Kyrou et al., 2018

claim: CRISPR-based homing gene drives have been developed in Anopheles stephensi.
source: and Anopheles stephensi (Gantz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gantz et al., 2015

claim: CRISPR-based homing gene drives minimally consist of a Cas9 endonuclease and a guide RNA (gRNA) cassette.
source: All of these CRISPR-based homing gene drives minimally consist of a Cas9 endonuclease, which facilitates the genome integration of the gene drive and a guide RNA (gRNA) cassette, which encodes the sequence-specific integration site targeted by Cas9.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about CRISPR gene drive components

claim: A gene-drive system has not yet been developed in Ae. aegypti prior to this study.
source: Unfortunately, a gene-drive system has yet to be developed in Ae. aegypti, the lack of which is principally due to the absence of tools necessary to engineer drives.
evidence: Statement of the state of the field prior to this work

claim: The authors developed split gene drives with a molecularly unlinked endonuclease to allow spatial and temporal confinement of the drive.
source: As a safety precaution, we engineered 'split gene drives (referred to as split drives from hereon)' with a molecularly unlinked endonuclease, thereby allowing the user to spatially and temporally confine the drive (Akbari et al., 2015a; Champer et al., 2016; Committee on Gene Drive Research in Non-Human Organisms: Recommendations for Responsible Conduct, Board on Life Sciences, Division on Earth and Life Studies, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akbari et al., 2015a; Champer et al., 2016; Committee on Gene Drive Research in Non-Human Organisms: Recommendations for Responsible Conduct, Board on Life Sciences, Division on Earth and Life Studies, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014

claim: The authors achieved cleavage rates indicating biallelic cutting of up to 100%.
source: To improve drive efficiency, we targeted a highly conserved region in a phenotypic gene with cleavage rates, indicating biallelic cutting, of 100%
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The authors achieved homing rates as high as 94%.
source: and homing rates, indicating the super-Mendelian transmission rate of the drive, as high as 94%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mathematical models predict that split drives could spread anti-pathogen effector genes into wild populations in a safe, confinable and reversible manner.
source: With cleavage rates up to 100% and transmission rates as high as 94%, mathematical models predict that these systems could spread anti-pathogen effector genes into wild populations in a safe, confinable and reversible manner appropriate for field trials and effective for controlling disease.
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript

claim: The white gene (AAEL016999) is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter.
source: We targeted an easily screenable gene with consistent and viable disrupted phenotype, the white gene (AAEL016999), which is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter (Bhalla, 1968; Coates et al., 1997; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhalla, 1968; Coates et al., 1997; Li et al., 2017

claim: A putative gRNA target sequence in exon 3 of white (gRNAw) was 100% conserved in 143 wild Ae. aegypti populations sampled.
source: From this analysis, we discovered a putative gRNA target sequence in exon 3 of white (gRNAw) that was 100% conserved in these wild populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis data and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B

claim: The gRNAw achieved a 92.7 ± 5.8% mutation efficiency in injected G0 embryos from exu-Cas9 females.
source: We achieved a 92.7 ± 5.8% mutation efficiency in the injected G0s, which is consistent with our previous work in this line (Li et al., 2017), demonstrating that this target site is accessible to Cas9 cleavage and that this gRNA is highly active.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from injection experiments

claim: Four U6 promoters (U6a-d) induced somatic loss-of-function variegated biallelic white-eye loss-of-function phenotypes in G0 embryos with moderate mutation frequencies ranging from 32.5–71.3%.
source: Of the six injected constructs, only four (U6a-d) induced somatic loss-of-function variegated biallelic white-eye loss-of-function phenotypes in G0 embryos with moderate mutation frequencies ranging from 32.5–71.3% (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Four U6 promoters (U6a-d) showed germline mutation rates ranging 27.6–67.5%.
source: These phenotypes were then scored in the G1 progeny with rates ranging 27.6–67.5%, indicating efficient germline editing (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–B

claim: The combination of the ubiq-Cas9 strain and the U6b-gRNAw and U6c-gRNAw strains induced up to 100% white somatic knockout frequencies.
source: Interestingly, the combination of the ubiq-Cas9 strain and the U6b-gRNAw and U6c-gRNAw strains induced up to 100% white somatic knockout frequencies, with varied rates of eye pigment mosaicism, indicating that these U6 promoters are highly active and timing appropriate when encoded in the genome to induce knock-out phenotypes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The white gene has been previously described as a sex-linked gene in Ae. aegypti.
source: This result is not unexpected as white has been previously been described as a sex-linked gene in Ae. aegypti (Bhalla, 1968), and recent genome sequencing has confirmed this linkage (Dudchenko et al., 2017; Matthews et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhalla, 1968; Dudchenko et al., 2017; Matthews et al., 2018

claim: The white gene is located in close proximity to Nix (AAEL022912), a dominant male-determining factor (M-factor) located on chromosome I.
source: as white is located in close proximity to Nix (AAEL022912), a dominant male-determining factor (M-factor) located on chromosome I (Aryan et al., 2019; Hall et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aryan et al., 2019; Hall et al., 2015

claim: There is little to no recombination in the white-Nix region, especially in males.
source: There is also little to no recombination in this region, especially in males (Fontaine et al., 2017; Severson et al., 2002; Toups and Hahn, 2010; Hall et al., 2014), which would further support sex-linkage at this loci.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fontaine et al., 2017; Severson et al., 2002; Toups and Hahn, 2010; Hall et al., 2014

source: Furthermore, modest super-Mendelian inheritance was observed (70.9 ± 7.8% in G2 progeny) which is significantly greater than the expected 50% for normal Mendelian transmission

source: while no cleavage or homing was observed from trans-heterozygous G1 male outcrosses to wt (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 3d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 3d

source: with an average 80.5 ± 5.0% inheritance rate in G2 progeny
evidence: Supported by experimental data from genetic crosses

source: while 51.0 ± 3.9% of G2 progeny from wU6b-GDe/w+; nup50-Cas9/+ male crosses had this somatic mosaicism
evidence: Supported by experimental data from genetic crosses

source: and 66.9 ± 5.4% of the G2 progeny inherited the drive (Figure 3E–F; Supplementary files 4c- 4d).

source: In general, the cleavage and transmission rates were relatively stable over multiple generations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

source: For example, wU6b-GDe/w+; nup50-Cas9/+ females transmitted white mutant phenotypes to 0.31 ± 0.07% of progeny that did not inherit both split drive transgenes, indicating that drive-resistant mutations were indeed generated at low frequency (Supplementary file 5b).

claim: Female fecundity was significantly lower in the nup50-Cas9 and the wU6b-GDe/nup50-Cas9 lines compared to the wt lines.
source: Female fecundity was significantly lower in the nup50-Cas9 and the wU6b-GDe/nup50-Cas9 lines compared to the wt lines.

claim: Cas9 expression is toxic to many organisms.
source: Cas9 expression is toxic to many organisms (Cobb et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2014; Wendt et al., 2016), particularly when it is expressed at high levels (Cho et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cobb et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2014; Wendt et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2018

claim: Mathematical modeling suggests that 10 consecutive weekly releases of 10,000 homozygous split drive males into a population with an equilibrium size of 10,000 adults would be sufficient to drive the split drive to a high frequency in the population (~97% having at least one copy of the gRNA/anti-pathogen allele).

claim: Mosquitoes with the gRNA/anti-pathogen alleles would be slowly eliminated, falling to a frequency of ~87% within three years of the final release.

source: This duration exceeds three years for the release scheme described above, and for fitness costs less than 10% in gRNA/disease-refractory allele homozygotes.

claim: The authors functionally characterized several drive components that performed with high efficiency in both somatic cells and the germline.

claim: Homing and cleavage efficiencies are largely dependent on the timing and expression of drive components.

claim: Maternal deposition can result in embryonic activity and the generation of drive resistant alleles.
source: and maternal deposition can result in embryonic activity and the generation of drive resistant alleles.

claim: Most antiviral effectors developed in Ae. aegypti to date rely upon small RNA pathway-directed targeting of viral genomes.

evidence: Supported by citations to Buchman et al., 2019; Franz et al., 2014; Franz et al., 2006; Mathur et al., 2010; Yen et al., 2018

claim: Small RNA pathway-directed antiviral transgenes are not easily multiplexed.
source: however, these antiviral transgenes are not easily multiplexed

claim: Arboviruses transmitted by Ae. aegypti have high mutation rates.

claim: Drive efficiencies are impacted by target-site availability, timing, the expression of drive components, host-specific factors such as the timing of meiosis and recombination, as well as the generation of resistant alleles.
source: Drive efficiencies are impacted by target-site availability, timing, the expression of drive components, host-specific factors such as the timing of meiosis and recombination, as well as the generation of resistant alleles that form as a result of non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) repair of CRISPR-mediated DNA cleavage as opposed to homology directed repair (HDR).

claim: Even imperfect drives with modest homing efficiencies are predicted to be quite invasive.
source: While these future drive designs are expected to be more efficient than current systems, it should be noted that even imperfect drives with modest homing efficiencies are still predicted to be quite invasive (Noble et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Noble et al., 2017

claim: Split drive technologies are a responsible choice for studying gene drives in the wild as they safeguard against spreading to non-target populations.
source: Safe, non-invasive, self-limiting split drive technologies, such as the systems developed here, are a responsible choice for studying gene drives in the wild, as they safeguard against spreading to non-target populations and will allow the assessment of potential risks and unintended consequences.
evidence: Statement based on inference from the properties of split drives

claim: Mosquitoes used in all experiments were derived from the Ae. aegypti Liverpool strain.
source: Mosquitoes used in all experiments were derived from the Ae. aegypti Liverpool strain (designated as wild-type [wt], Supplementary file 8a).

source: Of note, the Ae. aegypti reference genome sequences were generated using this strain (Matthews et al., 2018; Nene et al., 2007).

claim: U6 non-coding small nuclear RNA (snRNA) polymerase III promoters are ideal for gRNA expression due to their nucleus-associated transcription and unmodified 5' and 3' regions.

claim: U6 promoters have been used to drive gRNA expression in various species.

claim: The gRNA scaffold was modified to eliminate cryptic termination sequences.

claim: The U6d-GDe construct had an unexpected 276 bp insertion in the right homology arm.

claim: Heterozygous wGDe/w+ females transmitted the wGDe gene to their progeny at normal Mendelian rates.

claim: Rates of maternal carryover-dependent cleavage varied depending on U6 promoter (26–100%).

source: while wU6b-GDe/w+; nup50-Cas9/+ males did induce white cleavage in 48.5 ± 4.0% of progeny and biased transmission of the wU6b-GDe allele to 67.3 ± 5.2% of progeny over multiple generations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 5d).
